newsitem.title: KENYA: Roads, taxes called barrier to Kenyan horticulture.
newsitem.headline: Roads, taxes called barrier to Kenyan horticulture.

text.p: Kenya's Fresh Produce Exporters Association told the government on Thursday that poor roads and illegal local taxes were hampering growth of their business, the country's fourth largest hard currency earner.

"Major and feeder roads in growing areas are currently in very poor shape, making it virtually impossible to collect produce for export -- especially during the rainy season," FPEAK Chairman Simon Ethangatta said at a horticulture exhibition.

"Some local authorities are illegally collecting produce levies from exporters. Besides wasting time on the roads and increasing costs, the action is quite a nuisance as it takes a long time haggling with them through courts," he added.
Ethangatta spoke at the opening of Hortec '97, an annual Kenyan horticulture exhibition. Agriculture Minister Darius Mbela was present but did not respond to the FPEAK concerns.

Ethangatta also complained about procedures in remitting value added tax and other duties, saying implementation was extremely difficult and a backlog of claims by exporters ran into millions of shillings.

He said a system of reimbursement, offered as an incentive by the government, was lengthy and tied up exporters' working capital. He urged the government to abolish the reimbursements and replace them with direct remission.

Ethangatta said he expected liberalisation of the power sector to end power rationing, which often interrupted production and interfered with refrigeration needed to maintain the quality of perishable produce.
Electricity is rationed in Kenya and power authorities say the earliest this could end is July.

Kenya's fresh horticultural exports were 84,824 tonnes in 1996 compared to 71,758 tonnes in 1995 and 57,364 tonnes in 1992. It earned 10.63 billion shillings from the sector in 1995 but FPEAK did not give figures for 1996.
Horticulture is Kenya's fourth largest foreign currency earner behind tourism, tea and coffee.
